title: Ubon–Yasothon 2-Day Trip: Rocket Town & Isan Food | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A cross-province plan from Ubon Ratchathani to Yasothon, Thailand, broken down day by day: beautiful temples, the old Ban Singha Tha quarter, the Phaya Thaen complex in rocket-festival town, plus Isan restaurants that are actually open with real ballpark prices.

ogTitle: Ubon–Yasothon 2-Day Trip: Rocket Town & Isan Food
ogDesc: It's only about 90 minutes from Ubon to Yasothon, so you can take in rocket-festival town, pretty temples and an old quarter, then loop back to eat your way through Ubon. A detailed day-by-day plan.
intro: Ubon and Yasothon sit just about 100 km apart — an hour and a half by car — so they pair up easily into a single trip. Yasothon is the home of the rocket festival, with a walkable old quarter and several pretty temples, while Ubon is the bigger city where great Isan food turns up on every corner. This plan drives out to Yasothon on day one, stays the night, then loops back to eat in Ubon on day two before heading home — with the restaurants and sights that are genuinely open all laid out for you.

blocks.html: If you fly into Ubon and want a trip that doesn't feel same-y, hopping over to Yasothon is good value: the distance is short, the drive is easy (Highway 23, Ubon–Yasothon), and the two cities give you completely different moods. Yasothon is small and quiet, with the feel of an old town and the Phaya Thaen rocket legends woven through it, while Ubon is livelier, with good food for every meal. The plan below runs as 2 days and 1 night — stretch it to 3 if you want to add some of Ubon's nature.

items: Distance — downtown Ubon to downtown Yasothon is about 100 km, roughly 1 hour 30 minutes by car along Highway 23
Transport — a self-drive rental is the way to go, since Yasothon's sights are spread out and public transport is thin. Rentals in Ubon town start around ฿900–1,300 per day

Without a car — there are buses and minivans on the Ubon–Yasothon route for around ฿80–120, taking about an hour and a half, but once in Yasothon town you'll be relying on motorbike taxis or a ride-hailing app
When to go — to catch the rocket festival you'll need mid-May (in 2026 it runs 8–10 May); outside the festival it's a normal trip, and the weather is at its best from November to February

blocks.title: Trip-planning tip
blocks.html: If you're set on seeing the Yasothon rocket festival, rooms in town book out fast and prices climb, so reserve several weeks ahead — or base yourself on the Ubon side and just drive over and back on the day of the event.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Leave Ubon, head for Yasothon, the rocket town

items.activity: Breakfast in Ubon before you set off
items.note: Try the Vietnamese kuay jab (rolled rice-noodle soup) at Mintra, in town — it opens early at 06:00 and has been going for over 30 years. A bowl runs about ฿50–70, just enough to fuel a long drive.

items.activity: Drive out of Ubon on Highway 23 toward Yasothon
items.note: It's about 100 km and roughly an hour and a half. You can stop for fuel and a restroom break along the way.

items.activity: Stop at Phra That Kong Khao Noi in Ban Tat Thong
items.note: An old square-spired chedi with a lotus-bud top, tied to the legend of a son who killed his mother over a bowl of rice while hungry. It sits just before you reach Yasothon town. Free entry, about 30 minutes.

items.activity: Into town to pay respects at Phra That Anon, Wat Maha That
items.note: The temple that's stood with Yasothon since the city was founded. Phra That Anon is an important old chedi of the Isan region, and inside there's the Phra Kaeo Yot Nam Khang (Dewdrop Crystal Buddha). Free entry.

items.activity: Lunch at a proper Yasothon laap spot
items.note: Yasothon is known for richly seasoned laap. Try a local duck-laap place in town — laap, koi and tom saep run about ฿60–120 a plate, eaten with sticky rice.

items.activity: Wander the Ban Singha Tha old quarter
items.note: An old community in the centre of town, with Sino-Portuguese shophouses, cafés, rice-and-curry shops and plenty of photogenic corners. Easy to stroll and shoot for a good while.

items.activity: Phaya Khan Khak Museum and the Phaya Thaen complex
items.note: A giant-toad building over 19 m tall that tells the rocket-festival legend, next to Phaya Thaen Park beside the Lam Thuan. You can wander and take photos outside for free; the museum itself charges entry in the low hundreds.

items.activity: Check in to your Yasothon hotel, then find dinner
items.note: Hotels in Yasothon town start around ฿500–900 a night. For dinner you can go for riverside Isan food or a spot in the old quarter.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Catch a Yasothon café, then loop back to eat in Ubon

items.activity: A light breakfast at your hotel or a café in the old quarter
items.note: Ban Singha Tha has creamy-egg rice, coffee and khao soi to choose from. An easy way to start the day.

items.activity: Hit a photo-worthy café before leaving Yasothon
items.note: Options range from cafés in town to garden cafés out toward Loeng Nok Tha — like Rong Si Chaiyakul, an old rice mill turned into a multi-rai garden café with lots of photo spots.
The same route, about an hour and a half. Along the way, pick up Yasothon souvenirs like pla som (fermented fish), prayer beads and Khao Wong sticky rice to take home.

items.activity: Back in Ubon for a Vietnamese lunch
items.note: Ubon has an old Vietnamese community — try the red-pork rice, wonton noodles or nam neuang. Places in town run about ฿50–100 a plate.

items.activity: Pay respects and see the over-water scripture library at Wat Thung Si Muang
items.note: An entirely wooden scripture library built over a pond, blending Thai, Burmese and Lao styles — a beautiful piece of old craftsmanship and one of Ubon's finest. It's right by Thung Si Muang in the centre of town. Free entry.

items.activity: Stroll Thung Si Muang and sit at a café
items.note: The central city park that hosts the Candle Festival grounds, ringed by cafés and souvenir shops to drop into.

items.activity: Grab Ubon souvenirs before heading off
items.note: Mu yo (pork sausage), kun chiang and Isan sausage are Ubon's go-to souvenirs, with several well-known shops in town.

items.activity: Close the trip with mookata or a night market
items.note: Ubon has plenty of mookata (Thai BBQ-hotpot) spots and night markets — a good way to end the trip with a proper feed before you travel home.

blocks.text: Food You Shouldn't Miss Along the Way

blocks.html: Put these two provinces together and the food never repeats itself. Yasothon shines at laap and freshwater fish, while Ubon covers Vietnamese food, Vietnamese kuay jab and processed-food souvenirs. Here are the places and dishes that locals actually eat, ordered roughly by how easily they fit into the plan.

items.name: Vietnamese kuay jab at Mintra (Ubon)
items.blurb: A breakfast spot in Ubon going for over 30 years. The standout is the Vietnamese kuay jab — soft noodles in a clear, well-balanced broth — and you can pick thin noodles, wide noodles, old-style hand-cut noodles, instant noodles or glass noodles.

items.name: Yaso-style duck laap (Yasothon)
items.blurb: Yasothon is laap country. A local duck-laap place does the traditional recipe — duck laap, pork laap, mushroom laap, duck tom saep and duck om — eaten with hot sticky rice in a homey setting.

items.name: Riverside pla som and grilled fish, Yasothon
items.blurb: Yasothon raises its own freshwater fish, and riverside Isan places serve fried pla som, grilled fish and koi pla — fresh and not pricey. A good fit for dinner on day one.

items.name: Agave Vietnamese Cuisine & Café (Ubon)
items.blurb: A small spot with a nice feel in Ubon, with a varied menu — red-pork rice, crispy-pork rice and wonton noodles — ideal for a late-morning or lighter lunch.

items.name: Creamy-egg rice & khao soi, Ban Singha Tha (Yasothon)
items.blurb: The old quarter has local spots for creamy-egg rice, khao soi, rice-and-curry and noodles — handy for a refuel while you're out shooting the heritage shophouses.

items.name: Rong Si Chaiyakul café (Loeng Nok Tha, Yasothon)
items.blurb: An old rice mill turned into a multi-rai garden café, with flower gardens, a pond and lots of photo spots. A good coffee stop before you loop back, if you have time to explore the Loeng Nok Tha side.

items.name: Nam neuang & mixed Vietnamese food (Ubon)
items.blurb: Ubon has an old Vietnamese community, and the nam neuang places serve the full set — grilled minced pork, fresh veg, rice paper and peanut dipping sauce. A fun lunch, great for a group.

items.name: Ubon mu yo & kun chiang (souvenirs)
items.blurb: Ubon's signature souvenirs — firm-textured mu yo, kun chiang with just the right sweetness, and tangy Isan sausage to take home. Several well-known shops in town.

items.name: Yasothon pla som & prayer beads (souvenirs)
items.blurb: Easy-to-find Yasothon souvenirs sold along the roadside — fermented pla som with a balanced sourness, and sweet, chewy luk pra kham. Easy to grab for the drive back to Ubon.

items.name: Mookata & night markets, Ubon
items.blurb: Close out the trip with the mookata locals meet up over, or walk a night market for snacks both savoury and sweet. A satisfying, good-value way to finish before heading home.

blocks.text: The Standout Sights This Plan Takes You To

items.name: Phaya Thaen complex & Phaya Khan Khak Museum
items.blurb: A giant-toad building over 19 m tall beside Phaya Thaen Park, telling the rocket-festival legend. Great for photos outside; the museum charges entry.

items.name: Ban Singha Tha old quarter
items.blurb: Sino-Portuguese shophouses in the centre of Yasothon — easy to stroll and photograph, with cafés and local food spots.

items.name: Wat Maha That & Phra That Anon
items.blurb: The temple that's stood with Yasothon since its founding, with an important old Isan chedi and the Dewdrop Crystal Buddha inside.

items.name: Wat Thung Si Muang (over-water scripture library)
items.blurb: A wooden scripture library over a pond, blending Thai, Burmese and Lao styles — some of Ubon's finest old craftsmanship, right in the centre of town.

items: Yasothon is a small, quiet town — you can see the main sights in a day. The charm is in the slow pace, not the number of places, so if you like packing a lot in you may find it light.

The rocket festival really is a big deal, but it's only mid-May, when crowds are heavy, traffic is bad, and rooms are pricey and full — plan well ahead. Outside the season you can still see the museum and Phaya Thaen Park.
Public transport within Yasothon town is limited, so getting around is a hassle without your own vehicle — renting a car in Ubon to drive yourself is the better value.
Many Isan restaurants keep short hours and may close unpredictably, so it's safer to call ahead or check the shop's page before you go.

blocks.title: Stretch it to 3 days
blocks.html: If you have an extra day, spend day three on Ubon's nature — Pha Taem, Sam Phan Bok, or catching sunrise at Pha Chana Dai — for a trip that combines old towns, food and nature in one loop.

faq.q: How far is Ubon from Yasothon, and how long does it take?
faq.a: Downtown Ubon to downtown Yasothon is about 100 km. Driving along Highway 23 takes roughly 1 hour 30 minutes, and a bus or minivan is about the same.

faq.q: Can you do an Ubon–Yasothon trip without a car?
faq.a: You can, but it's more of a hassle. There are buses and minivans on the Ubon–Yasothon route for around 80–120 THB. The catch is that public transport within Yasothon town is limited, so you'll rely on motorbike taxis or a ride-hailing app. Renting a car to drive yourself from Ubon is far more flexible.

faq.q: When do I need to go to see the Yasothon rocket festival?
faq.a: The Yasothon Bun Bang Fai (rocket festival) is held in mid-May each year (in 2026 it runs 8–10 May), with parades, rocket competitions and rocket launches. Crowds are heavy and rooms fill quickly, so book ahead.

faq.q: What can you do on a 2-day, 1-night Ubon–Yasothon trip?
faq.a: Day one, drive from Ubon to Yasothon, stopping at Phra That Kong Khao Noi, Wat Maha That, the Ban Singha Tha quarter and the Phaya Thaen complex, then overnight in Yasothon town. Day two, sit at a café, then loop back to Ubon for Vietnamese food, pay respects at Wat Thung Si Muang, stroll Thung Si Muang, and pick up souvenirs before heading home.

faq.q: What are the signature souvenirs from Ubon and Yasothon?
faq.a: Ubon is known for mu yo, kun chiang and Isan sausage, while Yasothon is known for pla som, prayer beads and sticky rice. Both are easy to grab for the drive home.
